rationale: C25 plausibly supplied a material template because it uses the same Philippine Property Act of 1946 to authorize an identified administrator to exercise presidential transfer authority concerning property in the Philippines. The child adapts that same authorization machinery to multiple rehabilitation agencies and section 4 property, adding a possession-and-use limitation. C22 is a broader delegation precedent, while C18 similarly authorizes named agencies to execute statutory property transfers, but neither matches the child's statute and Philippine-property setting as closely as C25.

shared_material.child_excerpt: The Commissioner of Public Roads ... [and other named officials] are hereby authorized, as to their respective agencies, to exercise the authority vested in the President by section 4 of the Philippine Property Act of 1946
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The Philippine Alien Property Administrator is authorized to transfer to the Republic of the Philippines in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Philippine Property Act of 1946
shared_material.explanation: Both delegate presidential authority under adjacent sections of the same statute to designated administrators for handling property connected with the Philippines.

shared_material.child_excerpt: Provided, that this authority shall be exercised only with respect to property located in the Philippines in the possession and control of the respective agencies
shared_material.parent_excerpt: property, or proceeds thereof, vested in or transferred to him pursuant to the Trading with the Enemy Act, as amended, and the Philippine Property Act of 1946
shared_material.explanation: Each limits the delegated authority by identifying the covered Philippine-related property and its administrative custody or statutory source.
